summary:
Tombaugh is a web-based multi-epoch viewer for NASA SPHEREx data. Given a star name or sky coordinates, it gathers every SPHEREx observation of that field and presents them as a time-ordered blink comparison, as Clyde Tombaugh did when he discovered Pluto in 1930.

SPHEREx maps the full sky every six months at 0.75-5 µm. Because the same detector sees a given field at nearly the same wavelength on each pass, differences between frames almost fully reflect changes in the sky rather than in the instrument. Tombaugh exploits this with blinking, differencing and false-colour views. It uses Gaia DR3 and SkyBoT to separate known movers from unexplained changes. Selecting any pixel returns a light curve and a spectrum, with molecular absorption bands (H2O, CO, CH4, CO2, ices) marked.

We validated it on Barnard’s Star (10.39″/yr, a clear difference pair), Epsilon Indi B (4.51″/yr recovered at 39σ), R Draconis and RW Aurigae (variability), and WISE 0855.

SPHEREx’s archive is large and difficult to explore directly. Tombaugh needs no download or installation and every view is a link that can be shared. This makes SPHEREx time-domain analysis easily accessible to anyone, be it students, amateurs or researchers.
details:
What it does

Tombaugh is a web viewer for NASA SPHEREx data. A user types a star name or coordinates (field of view 1′ to 120′). The system finds every SPHEREx Level 2 exposure covering that spot and shows how the field changes between visits. SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, so a given patch has been imaged several times, months apart. Tombaugh turns those repeat visits into a flip-book, the technique Clyde Tombaugh used in 1930 to find Pluto.

It has four main views and an experimental moving-object search:

- Blink: shows frames from one detector, in time order, on a common north-up grid. Users can choose playback speed from 0.5 to 4 frames per second.

- Difference: each frame minus the frame furthest from it in time, after removing each frame's own sky level. Stationary stars thus cancel out to grey while a moving one leaves a white spot (now) beside a dark one (then).

- Colour: one false-colour image per pass: blue for 0.75 to 1.6 µm, green for 1.6 to 3.8 µm, red for 3.8 to 5 µm. For example cold brown dwarfs, which faint at short wavelengths, look red.

- Pixel inspector: clicking any pixel returns aperture photometry across every covering frame. The result is thus a light curve and a spectrum with the bands of H2O, CO, CH4, CO2 and ices marked.

- Moving-object search (experimental): for one visit, the server looks for sources that shift between the bursts of frames (2 to 4 frames about 2 minutes apart, bursts hours apart), links them into tracks, and matches each track against SkyBoT. Known asteroids and comets are labelled with their names; unmatched tracks are shown as candidates. It searches the central 30′ of the field and takes about a minute.

How it works

Each SPHEREx detector sees a given spot at nearly the same wavelength on every pass. Between visits, the sky changes (and the instrument does not). We rely on this and it is why we blink one detector at a time instead of mixing wavelengths.

A Python server finds the frames through an index built from IRSA's catalogue. It reads only the needed rows of each file straight from IRSA's cloud copy, using HTTP range requests, so there are no full downloads (to improve latency). It then masks bad pixels using the pipeline's flag bits, which we checked against real frames. It regrids to north-up and streams frames to the browser as they are ready. The browser does the differencing and colour maths. The URL encodes the whole view, so any view can be shared or embedded in an iframe on another website.

Benefits and intended impact

SPHEREx's archive is large and awkward to explore directly. Tombaugh requires no download, installation or knowledge of FITS formatting. That makes time-domain exploration of SPHEREx data possible for students and educators (a one-click demonstration of proper motion and variability), amateur astronomers, or even perhaps researchers who want a quick look before committing to analysis. Shareable URLs and an embeddable viewer make it easy for others to reuse the tool. A weekly refresh script adds frames from new SPHEREx releases with no code changes.

Tools and technologies

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS

- Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, reproject, DuckDB and PyArrow (catalogue index), httpx

- Data: SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images (IRSA, releases QR1 to QR3), Gaia DR3, SIMBAD (CfA mirror), IMCCE SkyBoT

- Deployment: a static site on Cloudflare Pages (auto-deployed by GitHub Actions) and the API on a Google Cloud VM behind Caddy with HTTPS

Validation

- Barnard's Star: moves 1 to 2 pixels between passes, seen in five of six detectors

- Epsilon Indi B: motion is under a pixel per pass, so it is very subtle by eye

- R Draconis (Mira variable) and RW Aurigae (young variable): light curves from 2,358 and 320 frame measurements, plus spectra

- WISE 0855: at 6″ pixels it blends with a G 16.3 star 7″ away

Creativity

The idea is a 1930 technique applied to a 2025 space telescope, using SPHEREx's all-sky repeat coverage. Some choices we made include

- using detector-by-detector comparison so changes in the sky are not confused with changes in wavelength

- having a two-purpose treatment of flags. The measurements exclude flagged pixels while the picture shows them, because most flagged pixels are close to their clean neighbours. And a separate overlay shows users where the flags are.

- using range reads from the cloud archive, which allows for fast querying without needing to mirror the whole archive

Limitations

- Saturated stars give lower bounds to the spectra. For example 2,356 of R Dra's 2,358 points are lower bounds, so its light curve is truly just a floor

- The spectra mix dates so a variable star like R Dra's spectrum scatters

- The moving-object search is experimental. It misses faint objects and ones passing over bright stars, so an empty result does not mean nothing is there. Unmatched tracks are candidates, not discoveries

- The colours are purely indicative and not flux-calibrated
